traps.trap: Posterior duodenal wall or lesser curvature is the commonest perforation site; posterior DU perforates (merged with TR2: wrong artery for the posterior DU bleed)

probes.stem_idea: Most common site of peptic ulcer perforation?
probes.correct: Anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum
distractor_set: Posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum
Lesser curvature of the stomach
Pyloric channel
probes.note: the trap is the posterior wall, which is where duodenal ulcers bleed

probes.stem_idea: Two duodenal ulcers: one presents with haematemesis and melaena, one with sudden peritonitis. Which pairing of wall and outcome is right, and which artery is eroded in the bleeder?
probes.correct: Posterior ulcer bleeds from gastroduodenal artery erosion; anterior ulcer perforates
distractor_set: Anterior ulcer bleeds from gastroduodenal artery erosion; posterior ulcer perforates
Posterior ulcer bleeds from left gastric artery erosion; anterior ulcer perforates
Posterior ulcer bleeds from splenic artery erosion; anterior ulcer perforates
probes.note: artery-swap distractors carry the merged TR2 error; wall-swap carries the TR1 reversal

traps.diagnoses: Learner has no anatomical reason linking wall to outcome, so site and complication are stored as loose labels and swapped.
traps.first_wrong_step: Treats the posterior wall as the 'deep' site that must be the dangerous one, instead of asking what lies behind each wall (free peritoneal cavity in front, the gastroduodenal artery behind).

repair.strategy: E1: contrasting cases, anterior vs posterior first-part duodenum side by side, discriminating feature is what lies behind the wall

traps.retest: contrast probe in segment 2 or 3 on the bleed-vs-perforate pairing; again as a vignette in the exam-trap segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: site and artery are tied to anatomy. Recovered: wall-to-outcome link now anchored to what lies behind the wall. Stayed fallen: still swaps perforate and bleed; revisit anterior vs posterior duodenum.

traps.trap: Pneumoperitoneum is always caused by a perforated peptic ulcer

probes.stem_idea: Most common cause of pneumoperitoneum (and what the qualifier 'most common' means)?
probes.correct: Perforated peptic ulcer
distractor_set: Perforated appendix
Blunt abdominal trauma
Recent laparotomy or laparoscopy
probes.note: this probe sets the true superlative; the trap is only exposed on the second probe

probes.stem_idea: Erect film shows gas under the right hemidiaphragm in a patient laparoscoped two days ago with mild signs; what is the most appropriate reading?
probes.correct: Expected residual gas after the procedure; interpret with the clinical picture
distractor_set: Perforated peptic ulcer; take the patient to theatre
Chilaiditi sign; discharge
Perforated duodenal ulcer; Taylor management
probes.note: the learner who reads 'most common' as 'always' picks the first distractor

traps.diagnoses: Learner has turned a frequency statement into a one-to-one rule, so any free gas means ulcer.
traps.first_wrong_step: Drops the word 'most common' and keeps only 'pneumoperitoneum equals perforated ulcer'.

repair.strategy: E4: show the exact qualifier, then give a counter-case where free gas has a different cause

traps.retest: vignette in the exam-trap segment with a non-ulcer free-gas history
traps.report_hint: Avoided: respects the qualifier. Recovered: now reads superlatives as frequencies. Stayed fallen: treats 'most common' as 'only'; counter-cases needed.

traps.trap: Any gas under the right dome of the diaphragm is free intraperitoneal gas

probes.stem_idea: Erect film shows a gas shadow under the right hemidiaphragm with haustral markings and no peritonism. Which sign?
probes.correct: Chilaiditi sign
distractor_set: Rigler's sign
Football sign
Falciform ligament sign
probes.note: all three are true-pneumoperitoneum signs, so a learner who reads any right-sided gas as free gas picks one of them

probes.stem_idea: All of the following indicate true pneumoperitoneum EXCEPT
probes.correct: Colon interposed between liver and diaphragm
distractor_set: Both sides of the bowel wall visible
Oval gas lucency over the whole abdomen on a supine film
Gas outlining the falciform ligament
probes.note: the learner who has not rebuilt the true-sign set (E2 flavour) eliminates the key

traps.diagnoses: Learner reads location, not content, so gas in the classic spot looks identical whether it is in bowel or in the peritoneal cavity.
traps.first_wrong_step: Identifies the gas by where it sits (under the right dome) without asking whether it is inside or outside the bowel.

repair.strategy: E1: contrast true free gas with Chilaiditi: gas outside bowel wall vs gas inside colon with haustra, plus the clinical picture

traps.retest: which-is-not and a vignette with a well patient and an interposed-colon film
traps.report_hint: Avoided: separates intraluminal from free gas. Recovered: now checks haustra and the patient. Stayed fallen: still diagnoses by location alone.

traps.trap: CT is the first investigation, or erect X-ray is the most sensitive test

probes.stem_idea: Sudden epigastric pain and board-like rigidity; which is the first investigation?
probes.correct: Erect chest X-ray
distractor_set: CT abdomen
Ultrasound abdomen
Gastrografin study
probes.note: the trap is carrying 'most sensitive' into 'first'

probes.stem_idea: Which statement correctly ranks the two tests for free gas?
probes.correct: Erect X-ray is the usual first test; CT is the more sensitive one
distractor_set: CT is both the first test and the most sensitive
Erect X-ray is both the first test and the most sensitive
Ultrasound is the most sensitive and first test
probes.note: the ladder of tests: first versus most sensitive are two different questions

traps.diagnoses: Learner uses one ranking (sensitivity) for every 'which test' question and does not separate first from best.
traps.first_wrong_step: Reads 'which investigation' as one question, ignoring whether the stem asks first, most sensitive or investigation of choice.

repair.strategy: E8: ladder of tests with what each answers: X-ray first and cheap, CT most sensitive when X-ray is equivocal

traps.retest: second probe in a different form, then in the cold-evidence last segment as a vignette with an equivocal film
traps.report_hint: Avoided: separates first from best. Recovered: now asks which question the stem poses. Stayed fallen: uses one test for every stem.

traps.trap: PYQ key and current practice give the same answer for investigation of choice

probes.stem_idea: A PYQ-style stem: 'Investigation of choice in perforated peptic ulcer' with erect X-ray and CT both listed; which does the PYQ key expect and which does current practice favour?
probes.correct: PYQs expected erect chest X-ray; current practice favours CT for the most sensitive test
distractor_set: Both the PYQ key and current practice expect CT
Both the PYQ key and current practice expect erect chest X-ray
PYQs expected CT; current practice favours erect chest X-ray
probes.note: each distractor collapses or reverses the two sources

probes.stem_idea: Two stems: (a) 'initial investigation' in an exam key frame; (b) 'most sensitive test' with an equivocal film. Choose the pair of answers.
probes.correct: (a) Erect chest X-ray, (b) CT abdomen
distractor_set: (a) CT abdomen, (b) CT abdomen
(a) Erect chest X-ray, (b) Erect chest X-ray
(a) CT abdomen, (b) Erect chest X-ray
probes.note: the last option is the TR5 reversal, kept separate from the TR6 collapses

traps.diagnoses: Learner has memorised one source's answer and does not hold the two frames, exam key and current practice, apart.
traps.first_wrong_step: Assumes one answer serves every frame of the question.

repair.strategy: E5: teach both, 'PYQs expected X; current source says Y', and tie each to the stem wording

traps.retest: vignette probe with paired stems; last segment mixed-frame probe
traps.report_hint: Avoided: holds both frames. Recovered: now names the frame before answering. Stayed fallen: gives one answer for both; practise reading the stem frame.

traps.trap: A normal erect chest X-ray excludes perforation

probes.stem_idea: Sudden severe epigastric pain, rigid abdomen, tachycardia; erect chest X-ray shows no free gas. Next step?
probes.correct: CT abdomen
distractor_set: Observe and repeat the examination in the morning
Discharge with a PPI
Treat as acute gastritis with antacids
probes.note: all three act on 'no gas, no perforation'; the correct option is the only one that keeps perforation open

probes.stem_idea: Free gas shows on the erect film in only about three-quarters of perforations; what follows for a clear film?
probes.correct: A clear film does not exclude perforation
distractor_set: Perforation is very unlikely
Perforation is excluded if the film was properly erect
Perforation is excluded if the amylase is normal
probes.note: sensitivity below 100 percent is the logic behind the key

traps.diagnoses: Learner treats a positive finding as a gate: no sign on the film is read as no disease, ignoring the test's miss rate.
traps.first_wrong_step: Moves from 'free gas shows on X-ray' to 'no gas, no perforation', ignoring that a quarter of perforations show none.

repair.strategy: E4: show the exact qualifier (about three-quarters, not all) with a counter-case of a clear film and ongoing peritonitis

traps.retest: second probe numeric; cold last-segment vignette with a clear film
traps.report_hint: Avoided: trusts the clinical picture over a clear film. Recovered: understands the test misses cases. Stayed fallen: stops work-up after a clear film, which is a dangerous habit.

traps.trap: When the patient cannot sit up, a supine or right-sided view shows free gas

probes.stem_idea: A patient with a suspected perforation cannot stand or sit; which view is advised?
probes.correct: Left lateral decubitus abdominal film
distractor_set: Supine abdominal film
Right lateral decubitus abdominal film
Lateral chest film
probes.note: the trap is dropping the qualifier that the patient cannot sit

probes.stem_idea: Predict where free gas collects when a patient lies on his left side, and why that side helps.
probes.correct: Between the liver and the lateral abdominal wall, because the liver outlines the gas
distractor_set: Under the left hemidiaphragm, where the stomach bubble hides it
Over the pelvis, where it rises from the bowel
Beside the spleen, which outlines it well
probes.note: the learner who keeps 'right-sided gas' also keeps the wrong side down

traps.diagnoses: Learner remembers the usual film and drops the qualifier that changes the view when the patient cannot sit.
traps.first_wrong_step: Does not rebuild where gas rises when the posture changes, so picks the side from the textbook picture.

repair.strategy: E7: contrast the two settings (sitting vs lying) and derive the view from where gas rises

traps.retest: mechanism probe, then as a vignette with an immobile patient
traps.report_hint: Avoided: reads the setting. Recovered: now derives the view from posture. Stayed fallen: reaches for supine or right-sided by habit.

traps.trap: Free gas rises immediately, so the erect film can be taken at once

probes.stem_idea: How long should the patient sit upright before an erect film for free gas?
probes.correct: About 10 minutes
distractor_set: Take the film immediately
About 5 minutes
About 30 minutes
probes.note: the first distractor carries the gas-rises-at-once model; the others swap the figure

probes.stem_idea: A film taken seconds after the patient was helped to sit shows no free gas, but peritonitis is evident. Which step raises the yield?
probes.correct: Repeat the film after the patient has sat upright for about 10 minutes
distractor_set: Repeat the film at once with the patient standing
Repeat the film after 2 hours of bed rest
Take a supine film instead
probes.note: anchors the number to the reason: gas needs time to travel upward

traps.diagnoses: Learner understands that gas rises but not that it needs time to reach the diaphragm, so timing is unanchored and swappable.
traps.first_wrong_step: Assumes posture change instantly relocates the gas.

repair.strategy: E6: anchor the number to the mechanism: gas must rise through the abdomen, so about 10 minutes upright

traps.retest: vignette on the step that improves yield
traps.report_hint: Avoided: knows the timing. Recovered: tied the number to the mechanism. Stayed fallen: still swaps the waiting time.

traps.trap: Surgery comes first in a shocked peritonitis patient; resuscitation and antibiotics wait

probes.stem_idea: Hypotensive patient, clear diagnosis of perforation peritonitis; what is the immediate first step?
probes.correct: IV access, crystalloid fluids and nasogastric tube aspiration
distractor_set: Immediate laparotomy
CT abdomen before anything else
Consent and shift to theatre while fluids run later
probes.note: each wrongly places a later step first

probes.stem_idea: Order these: antibiotics and PPI, omental patch and lavage, IV fluids with NG tube, baseline bloods and group and save.
probes.correct: Fluids and NG tube, bloods, antibiotics and PPI, then omental patch and lavage
distractor_set: Omental patch and lavage, fluids, antibiotics, bloods
Antibiotics, omental patch and lavage, fluids, bloods
Bloods, omental patch and lavage, fluids, antibiotics
probes.note: the learner jumps definitive treatment ahead of resuscitation

traps.diagnoses: Learner ranks steps by importance of the definitive treatment, not by what keeps the patient alive until theatre.
traps.first_wrong_step: Treats the operation as the first step because it is the definitive treatment.

repair.strategy: E9: order the steps and ask what first and why; resuscitate so the patient survives anaesthesia

traps.retest: second sequence probe in management; cold-evidence vignette with hypotension
traps.report_hint: Avoided: resuscitates first. Recovered: now orders the steps. Stayed fallen: puts theatre before fluids, which is the unsafe order.

traps.trap: Non-operative (Taylor) management suits any stable or diagnosed perforation

probes.stem_idea: Stable patient, early presentation, a contrast study shows the perforation is sealed; which management?
probes.correct: Conservative (Taylor) management with NG suction, fluids, antibiotics and PPI
distractor_set: Laparotomy with omental patch closure
Laparoscopic washout alone
Partial gastrectomy
probes.note: a correct-conservative stem first, so the learner meets the qualifier before it is attacked

probes.stem_idea: Elderly patient on steroids with free perforation and generalised peritonitis; most appropriate management?
probes.correct: Resuscitate, then surgical repair with omental patch and lavage
distractor_set: Taylor method, as the patient is haemodynamically stable
Taylor method after an erect X-ray shows free gas
Taylor method without contrast, to avoid contrast risks
probes.note: all three drop the sealed-and-confirmed qualifier

traps.diagnoses: Learner has Taylor as a named treatment option and no condition attached to it.
traps.first_wrong_step: Drops the qualifier 'sealed, confirmed on contrast study, selected stable patient' and applies the name to any stable patient.

repair.strategy: E7: highlight the qualifier and contrast a sealed contained perforation with a free perforation with generalised peritonitis

traps.retest: second vignette; last-segment mixed management case
traps.report_hint: Avoided: checks sealing before conservative care. Recovered: now attaches the qualifier. Stayed fallen: applies Taylor to any stable patient.

traps.trap: The PYQ-key operation name and the strictly correct name are the same

probes.stem_idea: A PYQ-style stem: surgical treatment of a perforated duodenal ulcer; which is the keyed answer?
probes.correct: Graham's omental patch closure
distractor_set: Cellan-Jones repair, scored as a different operation
Simple closure without a patch
Billroth I gastrectomy
probes.note: the PYQ key says Graham's patch; the learner who knows the strict names doubts it

probes.stem_idea: Strict distinction: which omental technique uses a free plug and which a pedicled tongue?
probes.correct: Graham uses a free omental plug; Cellan-Jones uses a pedicled omental tongue
distractor_set: Graham uses a pedicled omental tongue; Cellan-Jones uses a free omental plug
Both use a free omental plug
Both use a pedicled omental tongue
probes.note: teach both: PYQs expected Graham's patch; strictly, a pedicled patch is Cellan-Jones

traps.diagnoses: Learner either believes the two names are interchangeable in every frame or knows the strict names and cannot map them to the exam key.
traps.first_wrong_step: Assumes the exam name and the strict name always coincide, or the reverse.

repair.strategy: E5: teach both, 'PYQs expected Graham's patch; strictly, pedicled omentum is Cellan-Jones'

traps.retest: contrast probe on the strict distinction; exam-trap segment keyed-answer probe
traps.report_hint: Avoided: holds both names. Recovered: maps key to strict name. Stayed fallen: confuses the two techniques.

traps.trap: Vagotomy with drainage or partial gastrectomy is the standard operation for perforated duodenal ulcer

probes.stem_idea: Stable patient with a simple duodenal ulcer perforation; which is the standard operation today?
probes.correct: Omental patch closure with peritoneal lavage
distractor_set: Truncal vagotomy with pyloroplasty
Partial gastrectomy with Billroth reconstruction
Highly selective vagotomy with repair
probes.note: older PYQ options remain in memory as the classic answer

probes.stem_idea: After repair, how is recurrence prevented in the modern era, and why is acid surgery no longer routine?
probes.correct: H. pylori eradication, PPI and stopping NSAIDs, since the causes are now treatable
distractor_set: Truncal vagotomy at the same sitting, to cut acid secretion
Antrectomy, to remove the gastrin-producing area
Lifelong H2 blockers with no eradication
probes.note: the PYQ key may still list vagotomy; teach both

traps.diagnoses: Learner has an old textbook view in which acid-reducing surgery is part of every ulcer operation.
traps.first_wrong_step: Applies the pre-PPI, pre-H. pylori logic of removing the acid drive surgically.

repair.strategy: E5: teach both, 'older PYQs offered vagotomy or gastrectomy; current practice is patch plus eradication and PPI'

traps.retest: mechanism probe on recurrence prevention, then a vignette in the final segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: current-practice answer. Recovered: knows both frames. Stayed fallen: still defaults to vagotomy; recheck the modern era logic.

traps.trap: Curling's ulcer follows head injury and Cushing's ulcer follows burns

probes.stem_idea: A patient with 40 percent burns develops a perforated duodenal ulcer; which eponym?
probes.correct: Curling's ulcer
distractor_set: Cushing's ulcer
Marjolin's ulcer
Meleney's ulcer
probes.note: the swapped pair is the central trap

probes.stem_idea: Match each stress ulcer to its trigger: head injury or raised ICP, and burns.
probes.correct: Cushing's with head injury; Curling's with burns
distractor_set: Curling's with head injury; Cushing's with burns
Both follow burns
Both follow raised intracranial pressure
probes.note: pair recall: Cushing equals brain, as in Cushing's reflex

traps.diagnoses: Learner knows the pair exists but holds the trigger-eponym mapping as an unanchored coin flip.
traps.first_wrong_step: Maps the eponyms by order of appearance, not by an anchor (Cushing links to the brain).

repair.strategy: E10: pair recall with an anchor, Cushing with brain, Curling with burns; contrast with the other pairing

traps.retest: contrast probe plus an eponym match in the final segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: pairs correct. Recovered: anchored by the brain-Cushing link. Stayed fallen: swaps the pair; review the anchor.

traps.trap: Shoulder-tip pain or tracked fluid is linked to the wrong eponym

probes.stem_idea: Perforated ulcer fluid tracks down the right paracolic gutter and mimics appendicitis; which syndrome?
probes.correct: Valentino's syndrome
distractor_set: Kehr's sign
Cullen's sign
Murphy's sign
probes.note: Kehr's is the common distractor offered with shoulder pain

probes.stem_idea: Left shoulder-tip pain after a fall; versus shoulder-tip pain in perforation peritonitis. Which eponym belongs to which?
probes.correct: Kehr's sign belongs to splenic rupture; the perforation shoulder-tip pain is phrenic referred pain, not a Kehr eponym
distractor_set: Kehr's sign is the sign of perforation peritonitis
Valentino's syndrome is shoulder-tip pain from splenic rupture
Kehr's sign belongs to perforated peptic ulcer, Valentino's to the spleen
probes.note: phrenic C3 to C5 explains the shared shoulder pain, which is why the eponym gets misattached

traps.diagnoses: Learner links an eponym to the shared symptom, shoulder-tip pain, not to the condition that owns it.
traps.first_wrong_step: Follows the shared sign (shoulder pain) to the best-known eponym without asking which disease owns it.

repair.strategy: E10: pair recall with contrast against the condition each eponym really belongs to

traps.retest: contrast probe and a later eponym-matching probe
traps.report_hint: Avoided: pairs each eponym with its disease. Recovered: now separates shared sign from owner. Stayed fallen: tags eponyms by symptom.

traps.trap: The period of reaction means the patient is recovering

probes.stem_idea: Six hours after a sudden perforation, the pain has eased and the patient looks better, with a still-tender abdomen. Interpretation?
probes.correct: The reaction phase; the irritant is diluted and bacterial peritonitis follows
distractor_set: Recovery; observe and re-examine in the morning
Spontaneous sealing; discharge on a PPI
Resolving gastritis; switch to oral antacids
probes.note: each reads the symptom improvement as the direction of the disease

probes.stem_idea: Order the classic stages after a perforation.
probes.correct: Chemical peritonitis, then reaction, then diffuse bacterial peritonitis
distractor_set: Bacterial peritonitis, then reaction, then chemical peritonitis
Reaction, then chemical peritonitis, then bacterial peritonitis
Chemical peritonitis, then bacterial peritonitis, then reaction
probes.note: predict-then-show: the acid comes first, bacteria follow over hours

traps.diagnoses: Learner reads symptom relief as disease direction, so the disease is running backwards in their model.
traps.first_wrong_step: Takes the dilution of the chemical irritant as healing instead of the lull before bacterial contamination.

repair.strategy: E3: predict-then-show; trace acid, then dilution and apparent relief, then bacteria

traps.retest: sequence probe, then a cold vignette of a late presenter who looks better
traps.report_hint: Avoided: knows the false-calm phase. Recovered: traces the mechanism. Stayed fallen: equates feeling better with getting better.

traps.trap: A patient who lies still has colic and one who writhes has peritonitis

probes.stem_idea: Two patients with severe abdominal pain: one lies motionless with a rigid abdomen, the other keeps rolling and pacing. Which has peritonitis?
probes.correct: The patient lying still with a rigid abdomen
distractor_set: The patient who keeps rolling and pacing
Both equally, as pain is the same
The patient pacing, since pain is worse
probes.note: pairs the movement sign with the cause

probes.stem_idea: Why does the patient with perforation lie still, while the patient with colic writhes?
probes.correct: Movement jars inflamed peritoneum and worsens pain, whereas colic eases with movement
distractor_set: Movement is blocked by pain in the gut wall muscle, as in colic
Shock leaves the patient too weak to move
Free gas fixes the diaphragm so the patient cannot move
probes.note: rebuilds the direction from the mechanism

traps.diagnoses: Learner has colic as the default pain picture and reverses the movement sign.
traps.first_wrong_step: Assumes more severe pain means more movement.

repair.strategy: E3: predict-then-show: what does movement do to an inflamed peritoneum versus a distended colicky gut?

traps.retest: mechanism probe, then a vignette in the final segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: reads still as peritonitis. Recovered: traced the mechanism. Stayed fallen: reverses the movement sign.

traps.trap: A perforated gastric ulcer is closed like a duodenal ulcer with no biopsy

probes.stem_idea: Which step is mandatory for a perforated gastric, but not duodenal, ulcer?
probes.correct: Biopsy or excision of the ulcer edge to exclude carcinoma
distractor_set: Omental patch closure with peritoneal lavage
Vagotomy at the same sitting
Postoperative H. pylori eradication
probes.note: the trap is treating patch closure as the whole answer

probes.stem_idea: A 60-year-old with weight loss and a perforated gastric ulcer; the surgeon closes with an omental patch and washes out. What was missed?
probes.correct: Biopsy of the ulcer for possible carcinoma
distractor_set: Vagotomy and pyloroplasty
A second look laparotomy at 48 hours
Gastrografin study on the table
probes.note: weight loss is a cue the learner must act on

traps.diagnoses: Learner thinks the operation is identical for all perforations and omits the one step that depends on the site.
traps.first_wrong_step: Reuses the duodenal pathway for a gastric ulcer without asking whether the ulcer might hide a cancer.

repair.strategy: E9: order the steps for gastric perforation and ask what is added and why

traps.retest: vignette on a missed step; last-segment mixed case
traps.report_hint: Avoided: biopsies gastric ulcers. Recovered: adds the carcinoma step. Stayed fallen: closes a gastric ulcer like a duodenal one.

traps.trap: Barium is the best contrast study for a suspected or sealed perforation

probes.stem_idea: Which contrast is used to show whether a perforation has sealed?
probes.correct: Water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin)
distractor_set: Barium sulphate
Air contrast
Lipiodol
probes.note: barium is the familiar GI contrast

probes.stem_idea: Contrast contraindicated in suspected perforation, and why?
probes.correct: Barium, because it causes severe barium peritonitis
distractor_set: Gastrografin, because it is hyperosmolar
Gastrografin, because it is radiolucent
Barium, because it is too quick to pass
probes.note: contrast the two media on what each does in the peritoneum

traps.diagnoses: Learner defaults to the familiar GI contrast and does not know which medium is safe in the peritoneum.
traps.first_wrong_step: Does not ask what the contrast will do if it leaks into the peritoneal cavity.

repair.strategy: E1: contrast barium and water-soluble contrast on what happens after a leak

traps.retest: which-is-not and a vignette on sealing in the management segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: knows contrast safety. Recovered: contrasted barium and Gastrografin. Stayed fallen: reaches for barium by habit.

traps.trap: The Boey score includes age, perforation size or bleeding, with delay 12 hours and shock below 90 (merged with TR22: Boey thresholds)

probes.stem_idea: Which is NOT a Boey score factor?
probes.correct: Age over 65 years
distractor_set: Shock on admission
Major co-existing medical illness
Delay to surgery
probes.note: age is a mortality factor in general but not a Boey item

probes.stem_idea: Boey thresholds: which pair of figures is right for shock and delay?
probes.correct: Systolic below 100 mmHg and delay over 24 hours
distractor_set: Systolic below 90 mmHg and delay over 24 hours
Systolic below 100 mmHg and delay over 12 hours
Systolic below 90 mmHg and delay over 12 hours
probes.note: merged TR22: number swap carried over from other scores

traps.diagnoses: Learner pads the score with general mortality factors and borrows thresholds from other scores.
traps.first_wrong_step: Lists every known mortality factor as a score item instead of recalling the three fixed items.

repair.strategy: E2: rebuild the three from the logic of risk (physiology, host, delay); anchor the figures

traps.retest: which-is-not versus numeric probe; last-segment recall
traps.report_hint: Avoided: knows the three factors. Recovered: rebuilt the set and anchored numbers. Stayed fallen: pads the score or swaps thresholds.

traps.trap: No board-like rigidity in an elderly or steroid-treated patient rules out perforation

probes.stem_idea: A patient on long-term steroids and NSAIDs has sudden epigastric pain, a soft but tender abdomen and mild tachycardia. Next step?
probes.correct: Image for perforation (erect chest X-ray and CT if equivocal)
distractor_set: Observe, as there is no rigidity
Treat as dyspepsia with antacids
Discharge with analgesia
probes.note: all three trust the absence of rigidity

probes.stem_idea: Which statement about signs of peritonitis in the elderly or immunosuppressed is correct?
probes.correct: Signs can be blunted, so mild signs do not exclude perforation
distractor_set: Rigidity is always present in perforation regardless of the host
Rigidity is more marked in the elderly
Steroids exaggerate the abdominal signs
probes.note: the setting qualifier is the discriminator

traps.diagnoses: Learner treats the classic sign as necessary for the diagnosis, ignoring the host factors that mask it.
traps.first_wrong_step: Uses the textbook picture of a young patient for an old or steroid-treated one.

repair.strategy: E7: highlight the qualifier and contrast the young and the steroid-treated host

traps.retest: contrast probe, then a cold vignette in the last segment
traps.report_hint: Avoided: respects the host qualifier. Recovered: recognises masked signs. Stayed fallen: waits for rigidity, which may never come.

dropped.reason: Merged into TR1: the artery-swap is carried as distractors on the TR1 contrast probe
Low yield; the 70 versus three-quarters quirk is folded into TR7's numeric probe and TR6 teaching
Merged into TR21: the thresholds are carried on the TR21 numbers probe
Low yield; laparoscopic repair qualifier can be a side note in the TR14 teaching

probe_plan: Backbone traps: TR1 (site and wall-to-outcome anatomy), TR5 and TR6 (first versus best investigation, PYQ versus current practice), TR7 (a clear film does not exclude perforation), TR11 (resuscitation before theatre), TR12 (Taylor qualifier), and TR17 (the false-calm reaction stage). Order: meet TR1 and TR3 early (site, then pneumoperitoneum with its qualifier); TR4 and TR5 together in the investigation segment, then TR6 and TR7 immediately after as the PYQ frame and the clear-film counter-case; TR8, TR9 and TR20 follow as investigation technique. Clinical picture comes before this: TR17 and TR18 share the mechanism segment (peritoneal irritation, direction of the disease), TR23 follows as the host qualifier. Management meets TR11 first, then TR12 and TR20 (Taylor needs a Gastrografin-confirmed seal), then TR13, TR14 and TR19 (the operation and the one gastric-ulcer addition). The Boey score (TR21) and the eponym pair (TR15, TR16) sit in the consolidation and exam-trap segments. Probes that compete in one stem are TR3 with TR4 and TR12 (free-gas reading), TR5 with TR6 (first versus best), and TR13 with TR14 (operation name versus operation choice). Every high-yield trap is first met at least a segment before its re-test, with TR7, TR23 and TR17 reserved for the cold final segment.
